Extensive experiments with OpenVLA-OFT across LIBERO and BadLIBERO tasks evaluate prohibited completion, physical incidents, and retained-task performance. On the evaluated LIBERO tasks, SAFI reduces aggregate target success after takeover to 1.3\%, with no recorded physical incidents or action saturation, while preserving high retained-task success.

title: PAD: Policy-Aware Data Valuation for Autonomous Driving
summary: End-to-end autonomous driving increasingly depends on scaling training demonstrations, yet data growth does not guarantee proportional gains. However, additional data do not guarantee better policies: a demonstration that benefits one planner may be redundant or harmful to another. Existing curation methods typically infer data value from intrinsic sample properties or training-dependent proxies that do not measure downstream policy utility. To address this, we introduce Policy-Aware Data Valuation (PAD), a framework that assigns each candidate demonstration a utility specific to the target driving policy. PAD combines scene-level calibration feedback with projected policy gradients and a regularized approximation of local training geometry, producing scalable influence-based values for the policy. A controlled group-removal study establishes the directional fidelity of these values, while cross-planner analysis shows that the same candidate pool induces markedly different rankings across planner families. On DiffusionDrive, PAD improves EPDMS over real-only training by 3.5 points on NavTest and 5.0 points on NavHard. Policy-specific curation consistently outperforms real-only and full-pool training across diffusion-, regression-, and flow-matching-based planners while substantially reducing scene-level regressions. These results establish policy-aware data valuation as a basis for replacing indiscriminate data accumulation with targeted policy improvement, enabling more efficient and reliable scaling of autonomous-driving systems.

title: Squoosh Bench: Evaluating UX-1 on 318 Historical Website A/B Tests
summary: Experimentation teams must decide which proposed website changes to test with live traffic. We evaluated whether forecasts from simulated shoppers could inform that choice. We screened 412 historical website A/B tests and evaluated four systems on the 318 that ran longer than 21 days. Each system predicted an original win, a variant win, or an inconclusive result. Page roles were masked and recorded outcomes were withheld during inference. Squoosh UX-1, a model fine-tuned on human browsing data, simulated 1,000 shoppers per arm and correctly classified 267 of 318 outcomes (84.0%, 95% Wilson interval 79.5-87.6%, treating experiments as independent). Qwen3 Next 80B, the strongest general-purpose configuration on outcome accuracy, correctly classified 196 of 318 (61.6%). UX-1 favored the variant in 126 experiments. In the live tests, 118 of those variants won (93.7%), four lost, and four had inconclusive results. The remaining 192 experiments included 19 additional variant wins.

AI Companies Develop Decision Models to Avoid Hallucinations
summary:
On 15 September, a startup called TypeSafe AI released a new AI model called Jev. The company’s broad, disruptive claims about Jev turned heads: The company claimed that Jev, which it calls a “System One model” is cheaper, faster, and can’t hallucinate.

TypeSafe AI’s marketing is an obvious shot across the bow of other AI companies and their large language models (LLMs), which, despite their capabilities in math and coding, are infamous for their cost and tendency to “hallucinate” factually incorrect replies. And the startup has certainly attracted both attention and investment. The company recently raised US $870 million in funding at a valuation of $7.5 billion.

But the most impressive metric of Jev’s success is arguably the many imitators it’s already spawned. Amazon, Cloudflare, Microsoft, and OpenAI quickly released “decision models” that imitate Jev’s capabilities. Startups, academic researchers, and independent enthusiasts have released dozens more.

“I have to give Jev credit,” says Matt Mastracci, an independent developer who has trained and released several decision models including Djev, which Cloudflare cited as an inspiration for its own decision models. “It really brought decision models to the forefront. In six or seven weeks, we’ve seen dozens of models come out.”

Jev’s Latency and Compute Advantages

Most AI researchers would call Jev a decision model or decider model. TypeSafe AI’s branding of Jev as a System One model refers to a theory of cognition popularized by psychologist Daniel Kahneman in his book Thinking, Fast and Slow (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2013). In the book, Kahneman draws a line between fast, instinctive thought (System One) and slower, deliberate thought (System Two).

TypeSafe AI argues that modern LLMs offer the second, but are too slow to provide the first. The company claims that Jev can provide end-to-end response latency between 70 and 500 milliseconds. By comparison, LLMs typically require at least several seconds, to provide a response, and more complicated tasks (like coding software from scratch) can take several hours.

Independent testing backs up TypeSafe AI’s claims. A preprint coauthored by Ramayya Krishnan, a professor of information systems at Carnegie Mellon University, along with several colleagues, found that Jev delivered a median latency of 150 ms across several benchmarks designed to gauge decision accuracy, including RewardBench and JudgeBench. OpenAI’s most capable model at the time, GPT-6 Astra, delivered a median latency of 1.89 seconds.

A faster reply is often a cheaper reply, because it requires less compute time, and that’s reflected in TypeSafe AI’s pricing. The startup charges $0.042 per million input tokens; output tokens are free. By contrast, for GPT-6 Astra, ChatGPT charges $10 per million input tokens; $50 per million output tokens. Even GPT-6 Luna, a variant of GPT-6 designed for fast, inexpensive inference, costs $0.10 per million input tokens; $0.50 per million output tokens.

Mastracci says that lower latency and costs open opportunities to tackle tasks LLMs currently can’t handle.“You can think of content moderation, such as moderating a fire hose of social media posts or an extremely busy chat room.”

Michelle Chen, a group product manager at Cloudflare (which has released its own decision models, including Clef and Claric), is also bullish on what decision models can accomplish. “You can probably offload 80 percent of your typical LLM tasks to a System One model that is going to be so much faster and so much cheaper.”

TypeSafe AI has offered few details about how Jev achieves its speed, but Jev’s open-weights imitators provide more transparency.

For example, take Cloudflare’s Clef, an open-weights decision model which is free to download on Hugging Face. “With an LLM, when you’re generating an output token, it looks at all the previous tokens and predicts the next output token,” explains Chen. This occurs in sequence, token after token, until an end token is reached. “Our decision models don’t do that. They just do a single forward pass, to generate one read of all the inputs, and then generate one output. That’s why it’s a lot faster.”

How Decision Models Generalize Tasks

Decision models based on an LLM, such as Clef (which is based on Alibaba’s Qwen LLM), still contain the neurons and transformer-based model architecture of an LLM. They still input and output tokens.

However, the portions of the model that turn these tokens into text have been changed to constrain the output. “Jev can only answer questions with a predefined, structured answer format,” says Zhongyu Wei, a professor at Fudan University, in Shanghai, who is also a coauthor of a study that benchmarks decision models and introduces an open-weight alternative, SII-Decision. “We give it a question and options such as A, B, and C, and it must choose from those options, returning probabilities alongside its choice.”

In one sense, decision models are a return to classifiers, a type of model that, as the name implies, learn to sort data into classes. They’re used in a wide range of tasks, including spam filters and face detection. “These kinds of models are not new,” says Chen. “It’s almost like a rebranding.”

But decision models offer a key upgrade over prior classifiers: generalization.

Independent developer Mastracci explains that classifiers were traditionally created through domain-specific training. Decision models, though, retain the general intelligence of an LLM, and that makes them applicable to many situations. “You can pick it up off the shelf, you point it at your problem, and it works,” says Mastracci.

Cloudflare is putting this advantage into practice. Before decision models, teams looking to use a classifier model had to “get a lot of data, stand up a machine learning team, and fine-tune” a model for the task, Chen says. Decision models eliminate this requirement, so one decision model can be used in many domains. Examples include flagging spam pull requests in Cloudflare’s GitHub documentation repository, catching spam and phishing emails, spotting phishing domains, detecting prompt-injection attacks on LLMs, and reading emails about internet-backbone outages to judge whether they’ll affect Cloudflare’s services.

Decision models are well suited for quick judgements on data like emails, messages, or documents.Source: TypeSafe AI

Do Decision Models Really Stop Hallucinations?

In programming, “type-safe” languages are designed so that operations mixing incompatible kinds of data—adding a number to a string, say—are rejected before the program runs rather than producing a bad result later. Decision models are similar in that they prevent the model from generating an unexpected reply. TypeSafe AI’s name makes the connection between type-safe programming and decision models part of the company’s marketing, and it builds on that to make a startling claim: Jev will never hallucinate.

This is, strictly speaking, true. LLMs hallucinate because they calculate probabilities for tokens repeatedly across a huge vocabulary of possibilities and output many tokens. This leaves room for less probable tokens to lead a response astray, or for the model to deliver tokens that are probable based on the model’s training but not correct in the context of the reply. Decision models, by contrast, calculate probabilities only among the predetermined possibilities, and the most probable is chosen. This eliminates hallucination.

However, Carnegie Mellon’s Krishnan cautions that “eliminating hallucinations in the output does not eliminate errors in decision-making.” He and his coauthors tested Jev by asking it to determine if answers to questions were correct. Jev performed well when the judgment could be easily reached by reading the prompt, but performance dropped off when the judgment required math or involved a logic puzzle.

Wei of Fudan University and his coauthors report similar results in their own research. They found the best decision models can slightly beat the accuracy of LLMs when asked questions about document understanding and score close to LLMs when asked questions related to tool use (such as choosing the correct software tool to call to perform a user’s task). However, decision models fall behind when asked questions in domains that require topic expertise, including medicine, finance, and law.

“I think reasoning is a key factor,” says Wei. Reasoning allows an LLM to work though its response before it provides a final answer to the user. However, Wei adds that reasoning alone doesn’t explain the domain gaps in all cases, as some LLMs performed well even without reasoning. Wei says the methods used to train decision models can also be a factor, and used decision-specific training for SII-Decision.

Yet decision models and LLMs don’t have to be competitors. Krishnan and his colleagues also tested by passing Jev’s low-confidence answers to GPT-6 for additional consideration. The combination of models slightly beat the accuracy of GPT-6 alone and did so at 41 percent of the cost.

Wei thinks this “hybrid architecture” will become common. “The decision model can call an LLM to give a more detailed explanation. And an LLM can call a decision model for a quick judgment. I think that’s very flexible.”

title: CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
summary:
CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

  • CVE-2025-42884 SAP NetWeaver Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Data Query Logic Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-76466 Cisco Expressway Series Use of Hard-coded Credentials Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-123890 VMWare vCenter Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-129448 Apache Roller Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. 

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. 

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. 

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

  • Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.
  • Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.
  • When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks:

  • Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages.
  • Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams.
  • Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks.

No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time.

Vulnerabilities

Expand All +
CVE-2026-117659
The InfoScan Electron desktop client improperly handles TLS certificate errors by accepting certificates without validating their trustworthiness. The client also configures Electron with nodeIntegration enabled, contextIsolation disabled, and webSecurity disabled. These settings weaken the client’s security boundaries. An attacker who is able to intercept or manipulate network communications may be able to present an untrusted certificate without the application rejecting the connection.

Product Status: known_affected

If you are an offline customer (InfoScan has no internet access), you will need to download the update from the Dorsett Controls Customer Portal by selecting the InfoScan Update tile, downloading the update, and following the instructions listed on the portal.

Mendix Studio Pro 11 >= V11.15.0 < V11.16.0

Product Status: known_affected

Maintain strict inbound firewall policies (such as Windows Defender Firewall) blocking external traffic on port 7782. This is already the case by default on standard Windows installations. If remote access is required, restrict traffic via a secure, authenticated channel (e.g., a VPN or SSH tunnel) rather than opening direct inbound firewall rules.

Update to V11.16.0 or later version

title: Critical Java Vulnerability Requires Immediate Patching
summary:
Purpose

CISA strongly urges organizations to immediately patch the recently disclosed Oracle Java vulnerability CVE-2026-114938. This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK). Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution.

Actions to take

CISA urges organizations to take the following actions:

  • Identify affected Java installations. Review your software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications or included in container images and appliances. Note: JDKs and Java runtimes may not appear as separate entries in software inventories.
  • Apply relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they are available, prioritizing internet-facing systems.
    • If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access.
  • Review Oracle’s security advisory for guidance on patching and affected products and versions.
  •  Monitor for indicators of suspicious activity, including rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes, and suspicious Java processes.

Resources

CISA urges network defenders to review the following resource and apply necessary updates:

Vendor Guidance

  • Oracle’s Security Advisory: Critical Security Patch Update – November 2026

  • Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.

  • When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

title: CISA Adds One Known Exploited Vulnerability to Catalog
summary:
CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

  • CVE-2026-115731 Perforce Puppet Enterprise Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability

This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.
